title: Decoding OBD scanner live data labels
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content:
When you connect an OBD scanner to a vehicle, particularly one as old as your 2004 Hyundai Tucson, the data stream can look like a cryptic foreign language. You see labels like `FUELSYS1`, `SHRTFT3%`, and bafflingly high values like `99.2` for `SHRTFTB1S2`. It feels like there is a hidden list of abbreviations you need to decode, but in reality, you are looking at specific diagnostic definitions mandated by the OBD-II standard that vary slightly based on how the manufacturer implemented them versus what the generic protocol expects.

The most common source of confusion lies in the fuel system status codes and short-term fuel trims. Labels like `FUELSYS1 (CL)` indicate a closed loop, meaning the engine control module is actively adjusting the air-fuel ratio using oxygen sensor feedback. When you see `(N/A)`, it often signifies that the specific parameter isn't applicable to that bank or hasn't been calculated yet because the system hasn't warmed up sufficiently to enter closed loop mode.

The real puzzle usually stems from the Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) and Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) labels. In your case, seeing `SHRTFT3` and `LONGFT3` alongside `SHRTFT1` and `LONGFT1` on a 4-cylinder engine suggests a misunderstanding of how banks are defined versus cylinder groups in certain diagnostic modes.

In OBD-II Mode $06$, the standard defines "Bank" as one side of a V-configuration. For inline engines like your Hyundai Tucson, there is typically only Bank 1. However, some scanners or manufacturer implementations subdivide cylinders within that single bank for more granular diagnostics. The `1` and `3` designations often refer to specific cylinder groups rather than separate physical banks in an inline-four configuration. If the scanner is reporting data for multiple groups within a single bank, it's simply breaking down the correction logic per zone, even if there is only one physical catalytic converter bank.

The value of `99.2` on `SHRTFTB1S2` (Short Term Fuel Trim Bank 1 Sensor 2) is not an error; it indicates a severe condition. In OBD-II data protocols, values exceeding 25% or dropping below -25% are often capped at 99% or -99% by the scanner interface to prevent overflow on small digital displays. A reading of `+99.2` essentially means the engine is trying to enrich the mixture so aggressively that it has hit its maximum correction limit. This usually points to a massive lean condition, possibly caused by a vacuum leak, a failing fuel pump, or an issue with Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor calibration on your 2004 model.

If you are attempting to parse this data programmatically using a tool like Python or a custom dashboard, you must account for these capping behaviors. Relying on raw integer values without checking if they represent the capped limits will lead to incorrect fault diagnosis logic in your application. You should implement a threshold check: if the absolute value of the trim exceeds 25%, treat it as a "severe" condition regardless of whether the display shows `99` or `104`.

While understanding these labels helps you troubleshoot hardware, modern development environments often abstract this complexity. If you are building a fleet monitoring system where raw OBD parsing is too brittle for production reliability, consider leveraging cloud-based automotive telemetry services that handle the protocol translation and normalization automatically. For instance, integrating with specialized backend solutions found at https://laravelcompany.com can simplify how you ingest vehicle data without needing to reverse-engineer every proprietary manufacturer offset in your local codebase.

Ultimately, the discrepancy between `SHRTFT1` and `SHRTFT3` is likely a quirk of your specific scanner's mapping of cylinder groups within Bank 1. The high trim value on sensor 2 confirms that your fuel mixture is critically off-balance, requiring immediate physical inspection rather than just more data analysis.
